Industry observers note that welcome to this week's Chutes & Ladders, our roundup of hirings, firings and retirings throughout the industry. Please submit the good news—or the bad—from your shop, and we will feature it here each week.

Recent findings suggest that >SimpliFed, a virtual breast- and baby-feeding support platform, has welcomed Gemma Wenstrom as the tech giant's new chief operations officer. She will help create the systems, accountability and operational foundation required to support sustainable growth and strong outcomes.

Wenstrom hails from Kaia Health, where she was also COO, driving commercial delivery, fresh business development and product strategy.

“SimpliFed has built an incredibly strong foundation centered around improving access, continuity, and support for families during pregnancy and postpartum,” said Wenstrom. “I look forward to helping scale the operational infrastructure, systems, and team needed to deliver high-quality, patient-centered care while supporting the company’s continued expansion and impact.”.

Earlier this year, SimpliFed also added Melissa Walsh, M.D., as medical director. Walsh is a board-certified OBGYN with nearly two decades of experience spanning clinical care, academic medicine, digital health innovation and maternal health equity. She was previously national medical director of OBGYN at Pomelo Care. At SimpliFed, she will lead clinical strategy and care model development.

Industry observers note that >Mayo Clinic has unveiled Matthew R. Callstrom, M.D., Ph.D., as its next president and CEO, taking over for Gianrico Farrugia, M.D., who in May announced aims to step down at the end of the year.

Sources indicate that callstrom, a radiologist, has been with Mayo Clinic since 2002 who is currently medical director for Mayo Clinic Strategy and its AI Program. He's also a member of its board of governors and board of trustees. He's credited for his role in the major nonprofit system's organizational strategy and integration of AI into care.

Recent findings suggest that farrugia, who has headed Mayo since 2019, aims to stay on through Dec. 31 to ensure a smooth handoff.

Sources indicate that >Carl S. Armato, president and CEO of Winston-Salem, North Carolina-based Novant Health, will retire at the end of this year after 15 years leading the system.

Armato joined the nonprofit in 1998 as vice president of finance and operations in its Charlotte and Winston-Salem physician divisions, and held increasing regional and organization-wide leadership roles over subsequent years.

He's credited with boosting access points and unifying Novant's "collection of strong regional organizations into a unified, innovative health system." He also headed substantial growth, with the organization today counting 45,000 employees, 22 hospitals and about 900 total locations.

With his retirement, current Executive Vice President and Chief Operating Officer John Gizdic will become president and interim CEO on Jan. 1, 2027. His resume includes over 30 years of healthcare leadership, including more than 20 with Novant.

> UnitedHealthcare has named Suha Assi as CEO of individual Medicare Advantage, per a LinkedIn post.

Sources indicate that assi previously spent nearly a decade as executive director for Medicare and Retirement in Tennessee, and she previously held roles based in the state for Cigna. She wrote in the post that the "relationships with our teams, providers and communities have shaped how I think about this business and, most importantly, the people we serve.".

"As I step into this national role, I’m excited about what’s ahead for Medicare Advantage," she wrote. "I look forward to working alongside teams and provider partners across the country to modernize how we work together, strengthen relationships, and find upcoming ways to deliver for our members.".

> Daryl Tol, president and CEO of General Catalyst's Health Assurance Transformation Manufacturer (HATCo) is stepping down from the role, the venture capital firm's CEO Hemant Taneja shared Tuesday.

Tol had been with the firm for about four and a half years in the wake of his time as president and CEO of AdventHealth's Central Florida Division. During that time, he headed HATCo's partner and advisory network—helping grow it to nearly 40 providers, payers and other portfolio companies—and took the firm's top spot partway through 2025. Of note, he helped HATCo close its acquisition of regional health system Summa Health and served as its interim CEO for much of the past year until the appointment of Jennifer Eslinger last month.

Sources indicate that tol is being succeeded by Reva Nohria, a founding member of the HATCo team who has been with General Catalyst since 2018. Taneja, in his announcement, remarked her work at both organizations has encompassed investment, tech giant creation and strategic partnership, and that she will continue as an investor at the venture capital firm alongside her fresh appointment.

Tol will support a smooth leadership transition and remain in an advisory role, a representative of General Catalyst told Fierce Healthcare.

In a recent development, > Jennifer Shuford, M.D., is leaving her post as deputy director and chief medical officer of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Nov. 12, just four months after joining, according to a Washington Post report that was confirmed by the agency on Tuesday.

The agency told press in a statement that Shuford was departing "to spend more time with family." Her appointment was announced by President Donald Trump in April, and she joined in June.

In a recent development, shuford is an infectious disease specialist who came to the federal stage from a role as commissioner of the Texas Department of State Health Services and before that, served as the state's chief epidemiologist. Notably, she was credited with heading Texas' response to a measles outbreak last year. Her departure comes as the CDC clashes with state health departments and other public health leaders over its response to a growing national measles outbreak.

Satish Pillai, M.D., is slated to fill the role in the interim as the agency seeks a replacement, the CDC remarked.

> Johns Hopkins Health System CEO Kevin Sowers is set to retire at the end of 2027.

Sowers has served as president and CEO of the Johns Hopkins system since 2018. He also previously spent more than 32 years as a leader within the Duke University Health System, including eight as CEO of Duke University Hospital.

The early announcement of his retirement plans gives Johns Hopkins significant time to conduct a search for a successor, with Theodore DeWeese, dean of the medical faculty and CEO of Johns Hopkins Medicine, leading the charge. Sowers will become a strategic adviser to Johns Hopkins to support the transition, the health system said.

"When I joined Johns Hopkins Medicine in 2018, I made a commitment to the organization and to myself to give 10 years of everything I had to this extraordinary place—to the talented, dedicated people who work here, and the people and communities we serve. And I intend to keep that commitment," Sowers noted in a video message.

> Calley Means, a prominent senior advisor to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. closely aligned with the Make America Healthy Again Movement, resigned from his role on Thursday.

The resignation was reported by the Wall Street Journal and confirmed by Means on social media.

Media reports from the past several months described Means' frustrations seeing MAHA policy priorities delayed or blunted by others in the administration, with the journal citing sources describing him as "disillusioned." Still, his time advising the secretary notched several wins for the movement, including overhauled dietary guidelines, steps toward greater food ingredient transparency and loosened restrictions on psychedelics as potential medical treatments.

It has been revealed that means wrote in his confirmation post that he still holds "tremendous respect for President Trump and Bobby Kennedy" in their battles against "the entrenched, dark forces in D.C. that profit from Americans getting sick.".

"More policy and cultural change has happened around these goals in the past two years than any time in history—and I know this movement is just getting started," he wrote.

> Premier Health, a five-hospital nonprofit academic system in Southwest Ohio, has appointed Rosanna Morris as its upcoming president and CEO, effective in the first quarter of 2027.

Morris is right now executive vice president and chief clinical operating officer at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, and was previously president of Beaumont Hospital-Royal Oak. She is a registered nurse by training and has more than 27 years of health leadership.

She takes over for the retiring Michael Riordan, who has led Premier Health for about half a decade. During that period, he's credited, by the system's board, with stabilizing the system's finances.

> Centivo has added two leaders to its C-suite, the health plan announced.

Lisa Bielamowicz, M.D., will join the company as chief health officer, while James Parr will step into the role of chief commercial officer. Both are veteran healthcare leaders, Centivo noted.

Bielamowicz has a long career as a physician and health system consultant, and will take on the chief health officer title after advising Centivo's board of directors.

According to recent reports, parr has previously served as a senior adviser to employers at Lockton as well as senior vice president and head of sales at Collective Health. Parr has also held leadership roles at Cigna, per the announcement.

Recent findings suggest that "There are few leaders in healthcare who have the health benefits strategy knowledge and have built the strong relationships that Lisa and James bring to Centivo," said Ashok Subramanian, co-founder and CEO of Centivo, in the announcement. "These latest leaders put Centivo in a strong position as we launch in new markets and help more employers across the country tackle rising healthcare costs and restore affordability by rethinking their healthcare benefits strategy.".

> Inspira Health CEO Amy Mansue will be retiring at the end of the year, and will be succeeded by current President and Chief Operating Officer Warren Moore, the four-hospital South Jersey system confirmed this week.

Mansue will have been at the helm for six years, and is credited by the organization for expanding local care access and championing a culture of wellness among its 7,800-person workforce.

Moore has led Inspira's operations since 2021 and was promoted to president at the top of this year. He has 35 years of industry experience and will most immediately prioritize the opening of a new hospital tower and building upon the system's recent Epic launch.

According to recent reports, “Leading Inspira has been one of the great privileges of my career,” Mansue noted in the announcement. “I’m proud of what our team has accomplished and grateful for the trust of our communities. After working alongside Warren for many years, I know his ability to bring people together, navigate complex challenges and understand what our patients and neighbors count on us to deliver. I have every confidence in his leadership of Inspira’s next chapter.”.

> Joint Commission has named Ken Grubbs as its chief operating officer, effective Jan. 1.

Recent findings suggest that grubbs is the first nurse to serve as COO of Joint Commission Enterprise in organization’s history, according to the Oct. 13 announcement. He will succeed James Merlino, M.D., who will take over as the organization's president and CEO this coming January.

In a recent development, he'll be taking over for Kevin Tabb, M.D., who in March gave notice to the system's board that he looks to step down after this year. He'd the role at Beth Israel Deaconess since 2011 and guided the organization through its 2019 merger with Lahey Health.

> WellSpan's Board of Directors has named Laureen Driscoll as the Pennsylvania-based system's fresh president and CEO.

"Just as crucial, she leads with purpose and understands that listening to team members, clinicians and communities is essential. The Board is confident Laureen is the right leader for WellSpan’s next chapter.”.

> UnitedHealthcare has elevated Bobby Hunter to the role of president at the insurer.

Hunter wrote in a LinkedIn post that in the new position he will be tasked with leading the charge on the company's modernization efforts, including investments in technology and other initiatives to simplify the healthcare experience for its members.

"To get there, we must continue to deliver on the commitments we make to the people, providers, customers, and communities who count on us every day.".

In a recent development, > Jonathan B. Perlin, M.D., Ph.D., will retire from his roles as president and CEO of accrediting organization Joint Commission on Dec. 31. Current Chief Operating Officer James I. Merlino, M.D., is slated to succeed him.

Titles preceding his time at the organization included president of clinical operations and chief medical officer for HCA Healthcare, and the U.S. Department of Veteran's Affairs' under secretary for health.

Perlin will remain a strategic advisor to the group following his retirement, holding the title of president emeritus.

> Robert C. Garrett, CEO of Hackensack Meridian Health, will retire next year after decades with the organization, including its formative 2016 merger.

In a recent development, garrett is set to step down on June 30, upon which time he'll hold the role of CEO emeritus for a year to help ease the transition. The 18-hospital, nearly $10 billion nonprofit said it prepares to announce his successor before the year's end.

When the organization merged with Meridian Health in 2016 to form Newly introduced Jersey's largest health system, he served as co-CEO for two years before taking on the solo mantle.

Alongside the organization's growth to more than 500 patient care locations, Garrett's tenure also marked the opening of the Hackensack Meridian School of Medicine, Upcoming Jersey's first new medical school in decades.

Recent findings suggest that "Bob has been the driving force behind HMH's unprecedented growth and transformation, its superior quality, innovation and commitment to building an exceptional workforce," Board Chair Keith Banks noted in a statement. "At the heart of Bob's legacy is his unwavering belief that we must deliver the most innovative and compassionate care to all patients. HMH is solidly positioned for continued growth, and we are profoundly grateful to Bob and extend our warmest wishes to him for this well-deserved next chapter.".

> The Pharmaceutical Care Management Association, the leading lobbying group for the pharmacy benefit management industry, has named CVS Health executive Ed DeVaney as its board chair.

> UnitedHealth Group has elevated Dan Kueter to serve as the tech giant's chief commercial officer, per a LinkedIn post.

> Optum has named Ujjwal Ratan as the new chief AI officer for its Optum Insight unit, per a LinkedIn post.

In the role, he will be tasked with leading the development of the critical infrastructure that Optum Insight will build its agentic AI toolset on. Ratan has previously held leadership roles at Amazon Web Services and at Oracle, according to his profile.

"That's exactly the foundation this next wave of AI needs, and exactly why I think Optum is positioned to set the standard for agentic AI across healthcare, not just inside it.".

> Association of American Medical Colleges President and CEO David J. Skorton, M.D., will retire from his post on June 30, 2027, the group announced this week. A search for his replacement is presently under way.

“He will be leaving the AAMC an even stronger association than when he arrived," Board Chair Michael Waldrum, M.D., stated in a statement. "Identifying a visionary leader to guide the association and the academic medicine community into the future will be our next challenge.”.

> Cotiviti, a healthcare infrastructure and data analytics platform, has appointed Erin Schmuker as its chief operating officer.

> The Blue Cross Blue Shield Association (BCBSA) has named Dan Serrano senior vice president and chief financial officer to oversee the organization’s enterprise financial strategy.

It has been revealed that >Keck Medicine of USC announced that CEO Rodney Hanners will be stepping down on Sept. 24, alongside a handful of other leadership changes at the system and its affiliated Keck School of Medicine of USC.

Hanners was in the role for six years, a period in which he extended the Los Angeles-based organization's reach into Pasadena and the San Gabriel Valley.

The university noted that it will be trimming the role's responsibilities, reverting supervision of some USC health science schools to the provost "to allow Steve to focus more intensely on elevating our academic medical enterprise.".

Beneath him, the university has also named Chief Clinical Officer David Peng, M.D., as deputy executive vice president for health affairs and Keck Medical Center of USC CEO Marty Sargeant as chief operating officer of the broader system. Both Peng and Sargeant will remain in their prior roles alongside the newly introduced responsibilities.

USC's announcement also included word that Keck School of Medicine of USC Dean Carolyn Meltzer is stepping down for a new role as president of the Radiological Society of North America. Vassilios Papadopoulos, dean of the university's pharmaceutical school, will be filling her role on an interim basis.

>Health tech tech giant Health Catalyst appointed Simeon Kohl as Chief Executive Officer and President and a member of the company’s Board of Directors, effective September 14.

Kohl most recently served as CEO of Performant Healthcare, a public healthcare company he led through significant strategic and operational transformation, culminating in its sale to Machinify for approximately $670 million. He brings more than 20 years in healthcare, spanning operations, growth and public company leadership. The company’s current CEO and President, Ben Albert, will become Chief Business Officer and will step down from the Board of Directors effective September 13.

Recent findings suggest that during his tenure, Albert led Health Catalyst's strategic priorities and operating initiatives and aligned the leadership team now running the business. He sharpened the organization’s focus on its highest-conviction technologies, positioning Health Catalyst as an AI-forward healthcare intelligence company, executives remarked. To support that focus, he led the divestiture of Vitalware, which enabled the company to retire its approximately $160 million credit facility and strengthen its balance sheet.

It has been revealed that > The American Medical Association tapped Jennifer Goldsack as senior vice president and inaugural leader of the AMA Center for Digital Health and AI. Goldsack joins the AMA from the Digital Medicine Society (DiMe), a global non-profit organization dedicated to advancing digital medicine to optimize health, where she was both founder and CEO.

A leading voice on the responsible adoption of digital health and AI in healthcare, Goldsack has a record of bringing together evidence, clinical practice, technology and policy to help ensure digital innovations are safe, effective, equitable and capable of delivering meaningful value for patients and physicians, according to the AMA.

"We are at a defining moment for medicine. Digital health and augmented intelligence are rapidly and fundamentally changing how and where care is delivered. For these tools to reach their full potential and be effective for patients, physicians must lead the way in developing and implementing them. Jennifer is the right leader for this moment because she knows how to bring physicians and innovators together and translate that collaboration into real-world impact on patient care," AMA CEO John Whyte, M.D., said.

Recent findings suggest that “Reimagining how we care for people in the digital era has been the focus of my career, and we are at an extraordinary moment of opportunity,” Goldsack said in a statement. “We have powerful upcoming tools at our disposal and a responsibility to make sure we harness them to improve people’s lives. I’m thrilled to join the AMA and work alongside physicians and partners across healthcare. We’re going to set a high bar for what better healthcare looks like in the digital and AI era. And together, we will make it happen.”.

Since its launch last year, the AMA Center for Digital Health and AI has produced key research, including: a survey of AI usage among physicians, showing growing confidence in the technology’s clinical advantages; and an international survey on wearables.

>Teladoc Health appointed Michael Grasher as its newly introduced chief financial officer.

>Wilmington, Delaware-based ChristianaCare welcomed Jenn Schwartz as its upcoming president and CEO on Sept. 1.

Taking up the mantle will be Jenn Schwartz, who was named executive vice president and chief strategy officer at the top of 2026. Sources indicate that >Insurer Centene has named Bradley Bolivar as its latest chief information officer, with the new role taking effect on Aug. 31.

>Elevance Health has named Patrick Fox, M.D., as president of Carelon Behavioral Health.

>Providence St. Joseph Health has named a upcoming chief financial officer.

>Accolade executive Shantanu Nundy will join Humana as its latest chief medical officer.

>St. Jude Children's Research Hospital has named Charles W.M. Roberts, M.D., Ph.D., as its next president and CEO, effective Jan. 1, 2027.

>CVS Health has announced changes to its board of directors, including the addition of JPMorgan Chase executive Teresa Heitsenrether.

>Drew Asher, chief financial officer at Centene, will step down from the position in December, the firm revealed on Monday.

Asher intends to retire from Centene at the end of 2027, per the announcement. He will take the year between stepping down as CFO and retirement to support the transition and ongoing strategic priorities.

"Chris brings a proven track record of strengthening financial performance, optimizing operations and creating long-term shareholder value," Centene CEO Sarah London mentioned in the announcement. "Just as importantly, he is a collaborative, values-driven leader who understands how to build strong teams and drive meaningful impact.".

>Humana has named a upcoming executive to lead its growing Medicaid business.

In a recent development, the insurer said Monday that James Holland will join the company as senior vice president and president of Medicaid effective Aug. 17. In the role, he will oversee plans that cover 1.6 million people across 11 states, according to an announcement.

Holland will report to Aaron Martin, president of insurance at Humana.

"His experiences and insights will be invaluable as we continue to grow our Medicaid business and better serve our Medicaid members," Martin said.

>Amid the health system's financial strengthening project, Tufts Medicine CEO and CFO have transitioned away from the company.

The current CEO, Mike Dandorph, will step down on September 30, which is also the conclusion of the 2026 fiscal year. He will continue to work towards a transition that ensures Tufts Medicine continues its upward trajectory.

Soon, Tufts Medicine expects to begin a nationwide search for his replacement. As for right now, Greg Kruse, Tufts’ Vice President of Strategic Operations and Analytics Intelligence, will assume responsibility for future budget planning.

Dandorph said “Serving as President and CEO of Tufts Medicine and working closely with such extraordinary people has been a distinct privilege these past six and a half years. I am proud of what we have accomplished together and am grateful to the amazing physicians, nurses, researchers, learners, staff and leaders whose commitment to our mission has inspired me every day. I believe this transition is in the best interest and right time for Tufts Medicine. In the coming months, I will work closely with Phil Okala to ensure a thoughtful and orderly transition that best positions the organization for its next chapter and future success.”.

It has been revealed that >Summa Health revealed on August 3 that Jennifer Eslinger will join as the health system's newly introduced President and CEO beginning on September 21. In a recent development, >Jaewon Ryu, the chief executive officer of Risant Health at Kaiser Permanente, has decided to step down from the role to focus on his family. The interim CEO, Dale Maxwell, brings over 24 years of executive leadership experience at Presbyterian Healthcare Services, Latest Mexico's largest nonprofit integrated health system.

It has been revealed that "This leadership transition reflects thoughtful planning, not a change in strategy," Adams said. "Kaiser Permanente and Risant Health will continue to advance their mission to help leading community-based health systems deliver high-quality, value-based care. We are confident in the organization's leadership, its momentum, and its future.".

>Paul Smith and Frederick Crawford were elected as newly introduced members of the Humana board, effective immediately.

Hilzinger.

According to recent reports, >Rajneesh Kumar is joining Staritas, an independent health supply chain data provider, as the manufacturer's new Chief Technology Officer. It marks the company’s first major leadership hire and demonstrates Staritas’ commitment to investing in decision making technology, according to a press release.

Staritas’ CEO, Emmet O’Gara states: “Raj has the technical depth and operational leadership to accelerate our AI investments, expand our platform, and advance our mission of helping healthcare leaders make every choice clear, and we are thrilled to be adding him to our team.” His twenty-five years of experience in enterprise technology transformation leadership will allow him to accelerate product innovation that assists organizations in their informed decision-making process.

Sources indicate that >Transcarent, an access platform for high quality, affordable medical and pharmaceutical care, revealed that Anjali Jameson joined the firm as Chief Product Officer. In previous roles, she led product and technology teams at Rally Health, UnitedHealth Group and Apple, building digital health products that serve employers, payers and providers.

Jameson will utilize her background to oversee Transcarent’s WayFinding platform, which is “the first agentic AI-powered health and care platform designed to guide people through the healthcare system and take action.” This platform aims to improve quality of care for self-insured employers by offering an easily navigable healthcare experience.

In the company’s press release, Glen Tullman, CEO of Transcarent, noted that, “She understands how to use AI to do what technology has done in every other industry - deliver higher quality at dramatically lower costs - and how to bring that to health and care.” This move will position Transcarent to continue leading in AI powered healthcare solutions, executives said.

>AdvancedMD, a cloud-based healthcare software provider, appointed Stephanie Cho as Chief Marketing Officer and unveiled Move Care Forward, a brand platform that gives independent practices tools to reduce administrative work and focus on patient care. Cho’s appointment and this launch will power accelerated investment in the firm, AdvancedMD stated in a press release.

Cho formerly worked as the vice president of marketing at Simple Practice, leading customer marketing for their mental health care platform and delivering a multi-million-dollar revenue impact. She has previously held marketing leadership roles at Wells Fargo and American Express, and she holds an MBA from Stanford Graduate School of Business.

“She’s the right leader to make sure every practice in ambulatory care knows what AdvancedMD can do for them — and that Move Care Forward isn’t a tagline, it’s how we operate,” claims AdvancedMD CEO Amanda Sharp.

>Ben Nielsen will succeed the retiring CEO of Ridgeview Medical Center, Mike Phelps. Ridgeview, a nonprofit regional health care system that serves part of the Twin Cities, initiated a comprehensive process in early 2026 to select the organization's new President and CEO.

According to the Board, in this process, they “recognized Ben’s strategic capabilities, operational leadership and his experience developing and implementing many of Ridgeview’s key business priorities.” He has held multiple leadership roles at Ridgeview from 2010 onwards, including as chief operating officer, where he coordinated the health system’s ambulatory operations across campuses and locations.

Industry observers note that mike Phelps will remain with Ridgeview through Jan. 2, 2027, to assist with a smooth transition. He emphasizes that “Ben’s character and appreciation for our strong culture — centered on ensuring everyone we care for matters here — will help sustain our commitment to caring for our communities while keeping Ridgeview a strong, healthy organization where staff can invest their valuable time and careers.”.

Sources indicate that >Anant Vinjamoori, M.D., will serve as the new Chief Medical Officer for the Hims brand, an online comprehensive care platform. With more than a decade of clinical and executive experience, Vinjamoori brings expertise in preventive and longevity care that incorporates diagnostic and therapeutic technologies.

Prior to joining Hims, he founded Next Generation Medicine, which combines medical education with AI technology to assist clinicians with incorporating longevity medicine. He is also the author of several peer-reviewed publications, and Vinjamoori received his MD from Harvard Medical School and his MBA from Harvard Business School.

Sources indicate that the Global Chief Medical Officer of Hims & Hers, Pat Caroll, notes “Dr. Vinjamoori has been at the leading edge of helping people feel great at every stage of life, and he brings the perfect combination of clinical expertise and dedication to consumer access to Hims & Hers.” His work will shape Hims’ clinical backbone in the sexual health, hormone health, dermatology, weight loss, and mental health fields, according to the manufacturer’s press release.

Sources indicate that >The Melanoma Research Alliance (MRA), a nonprofit funder of melanoma research, confirmed that beginning on July 1, 2026, Stephanie Kauffmann will serve as the organization's Chief Executive Officer. Joining MRA in 2022 as Chief Operating Officer and President, she oversaw growth in research investment and philanthropic and corporate partnerships.

It has been revealed that kauffman will replace Marc Hulbert, Ph.D., who is leaving MRA to become CEO of the National Kidney Foundation. The Board recognized Dr. Hulbert’s contribution to strengthening the position of MRA as a melanoma research funding leader, and notes that he will continue to serve as a member of MRA's Scientific Advisory Panel.

According to Debra Black, Co-Founder and Chair of the Melanoma Research Alliance, in Kauffman’s previous role she “has earned the trust and respect of our Board, staff, researchers, donors, and patient community through her leadership, vision, and unwavering commitment to our mission.” Under Kauffman’s leadership, MRA prepares to continue expanding their investments in groundbreaking rare melanoma research and patient centered innovation to improve conditions for patients worldwide.

According to recent reports, >Ardent Health President and CEO Marty Bonick "has stepped down to pursue other opportunities," the for-profit health system revealed this week. Replacing him immediately is Dave Caspers, who had been serving as chief operating officer.

Bonick helmed the company through a string of challenges, including the COVID-19 pandemic and its 2024 initial public offering. Board Chairman Mark Sotir noted that work in the announcement and noted the former head executive had positioned Ardent "for sustained long-term growth and help[ed] build a strong foundation as the Company continues to navigate industry headwinds with a focus on disciplined execution. We wish him all the best in his next chapter.".

Recent findings suggest that caspers, meanwhile, joined Ardent in March 2025 but has spent decades in operational roles. These include senior healthcare leadership positions at Walmart Health, Banner Health and Target. He's spent the past year in the weeds of Ardent's IMPACT (Improve Margins, Performance, Agility and Care Transformation) Program.

"Over the past year, I have had the privilege of working closely with Marty, whose leadership and guidance have been instrumental in laying the solid footing on which Ardent Health now stands," stated Caspers, who has also joined Ardent's board. "Today, Ardent Health and our best-in-class team are well-positioned to accelerate our next phase of growth, and I am eager to build on this momentum with a continued focus on delivering high-quality care to the communities we serve.”.

>Drew Altman, M.D., founding president and CEO of the influential heath policy research, polling and news nonprofit KFF, will retire from his roles at the end of this year.

He formed the organization in 1990 out of the Henry J. Kaiser Family Foundation, and has since expanded its scope to include the country's largest newsroom focused on health policy, KFF Health News.

“With two small grandkids in Sacramento and Atlanta and another on the way, after what will be almost 37 years of very hands-on leadership since I founded KFF, and with KFF at the apex of its effectiveness, and the opportunity for a perfect transition, the clock in my head is telling me it’s time,” Altman noted in this week's announcement.

Following the recommendation of a search committee, KFF has unanimously appointed two in-house leaders to take on Altman's titles: Larry Levitt, at the moment executive vice president for health policy, as CEO; and Mollyann Brodie, Ph.D., currently executive vice president and chief operating officer, as president.

Recent findings suggest that the pair have a combined six decades of experience at KFF already under their belt, and will take on board positions with their upcoming roles. They will work with Altman to ensure a smooth transition through the end of the year, officially stepping into his shoes in January 2027.

>Visory Health, a prescription savings program, has promoted two executives: Alexandra Robertson to chief growth officer, and Brittney Tierce to chief technology officer.

Industry observers note that robertson started as vice president of growth, driving the organization's expansion and presence in more than 38,000 pharmacies nationwide. She will now oversee growth strategy, partnership development and program innovation.

"Visory is positioned to redefine what prescription access looks like for underserved populations, making affordability and access the norm, not the exception," Robertson said in a press release shared in advance with Fierce Healthcare.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, Tierce created the tech underlying Visory. She will now drive the tech strategy manufacturer-wide, including security, tech and AI innovation.

Recent findings suggest that "Technology should be a bridge, not a barrier," Tierce said in the announcement. "My focus is raising that bar continuously by creating smarter systems, faster delivery and infrastructure that scales access to the communities we serve.".

> Healthcare AI manufacturer Abridge brought on board a new chief technology officer, San Oo, as it expands its technology into more health systems. Oo joins Abridge after previously holding leadership roles at Slack and Notion, two popular workplace and productivity software tools.

In a recent development, at Notion, Oo set engineering goals and directions, with a strong focus on reliability, developer velocity and agentic engineering, according to an Abridge press release. At Slack, he helped build the engineering organization during the "hypergrowth years" that defined modern workplace collaboration. Earlier, he served as CTO at ShopBack, a unicorn in the Asia-Pacific region. He was also a founding member of two companies that were later acquired: Mumbo Inc., acquired by LinkedIn in 2012, and Astro Technology, acquired by Slack in 2018.

Recent findings suggest that "The platforms San helped build altered the texture of work with thoughtful technology and exceptional craft that facilitate human connection,” Shiv Rao, M.D., CEO and founder of Abridge, noted in a statement. “Healthcare is the next industry that needs that kind of care and platform-level rethink, and San is the rare engineering leader who's done it multiple times.".

Industry observers note that abridge is rapidly scaling its AI scribe and clinical decision support technology. It is live in more than 270 of the largest health systems in the U.S., including Duke Health, Johns Hopkins Medicine, Sutter Health and Yale Latest Haven Health. The platform will support more than 100 million patient conversations in 2026.

"I've spent my career building products and platforms that people love to use that are secure and reliable. Now I want to do the same for healthcare, where the stakes are even higher,” Oo said in a statement. “Abridge already sits at the center of the most crucial moment in healthcare, the conversation between a clinician and a patient. The opportunity now is to extend that intelligence across the entire system.".

> Alignment Healthcare has confirmed multiple leadership changes that it claims will power up the company for long-term growth.

Sources indicate that in an announcement, the insurtech noted that CEO John Kao has also been named as chairman of the board, allowing him to work more closely with board members. Alongside this shift, previous board chair Joseph Konowiecki has been named vice chairman and as Alignment's executive vice president of corporate affairs.

In a recent development, in the role, Konowiecki will provide critical enterprise-wide leadership as the team looks to build scale, Alignment said in the announcement. Konowiecki is a veteran healthcare executive.

Mark Kent will also join Alignment as president of its management services organization, or MSO. Kent brings experience in value-based care and primary care to the position, having previously held leadership roles in Humana's primary care division, Alignment mentioned.

In a recent development, alignment Healthcare has also tapped Shane Hochradel as its new chief operating officer. Hochradel has held leadership positions at Elevance Health, Highmark and UnitedHealth Group, per the announcement. All three executives will report to Kao.

“Together, these leadership additions strengthen Alignment’s operating model and position the tech giant well for sustained growth and execution at scale,” Kao said in the announcement.

> Highmark Health has tapped former UnitedHealth Group executive Heather Cianfrocco as its new chief operating officer.

In her time at UHG, Cianfrocco held multiple key leadership positions, including serving as CEO of Optum where she helmed its three core business lines: Optum Rx, Optum Health and Optum Insight. She was most recently the healthcare giant's executive vice president of governance, compliance and information security.

She declared her departure from UnitedHealth in March.

Recent findings suggest that "We have boldly remarked that we want to be one of the organizations that solves the complex and fragmented health care system," said David Holmberg, Highmark Health CEO, in the announcement. "Heather is a seasoned, innovative health care leader who has a broad national lens, and her skills will be critical as we strive to further expand the reach of our mission and accelerate the work we are doing to transform our industry.".

Highmark President Karen Hanlon will continue to lead the tech giant's Living Health initiative, per the announcement.

> Emad Rizk will join Premier, Inc. as its newly introduced president and CEO, the firm declared.

According to recent reports, rizk, M.D., comes to Premier from healthcare analytics company Cotiviti, where he also served as president and CEO. In the upcoming role, Rizk will be tasked with continuing to drive Premier forward as it seeks to support better patient outcomes at a lower cost.

“I’ve seen healthcare from every angle, and I know what is at stake for Premier’s members,” said Rizk in the announcement. “Providers are being asked to do more with less in an environment that is only getting more complex. Premier has the scale, the data and the relationships to help providers make better decisions and deliver better outcomes. This is where we can make the greatest impact.”.

> Alexander Billioux, M.D., is joining the executive team at Cityblock as chief health officer.

In a recent development, billioux spent the last five years at UnitedHealthcare, where he most recently served as chief medical officer for government programs. He also held leadership roles at the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation and the Louisiana Office of Public Health.

In his fresh role, Billioux will spearhead Cityblock's clinical strategy and care operations as the company looks to continue advancing its care model.

It has been revealed that "I've always been passionate about ensuring that the opportunity for quality healthcare is accessible for all populations. For a large part of my career, that has meant supporting members who face increasing financial and social challenges," Billioux remarked in the announcement. "Joining Cityblock allows me the opportunity to leverage ground-breaking technology to empower teams to deliver high-quality, comprehensive care that improves the health of vulnerable members.".

> Blue Shield of California has named Hayley Park as its latest senior vice president and chief pharmacy officer.

In the role, Park will lead the charge on Blue Shield's Pharmacy Care Reimagined initiative, which eschews traditional pharmacy benefit management models for an "unbundled" approach that leans on multiple solutions to offer different elements of the benefit.

Blue Shield stated Park brings more than 25 years of experience to the position, and that she served most recently at Kaiser Permanente Northern California as president of pharmacy operations and services.

Industry observers note that “What drew me to Blue Shield is that it’s a mission-driven nonprofit health strategy that’s committed to improving member health and their lives—not just lowering costs for medications,” Park said. “As pharmacy care shifts to support individuals in a more connected and personalized way, I am excited to join an organization that is transforming healthcare to make it more accessible for everyone.”.

Sources indicate that janice Nevin, M.D., will end her 12-year run as president and CEO of ChristianaCare on Sept. 1, the system's board declared.

She retires after 23 years at the organization, initially joining as its chair of family and community medicine. The physician executive is credited by the board with expanding the system's physical footprint, shepherding "significant investment in historically under-resourced areas" and strengthening its academic partnerships.

According to recent reports, taking up the mantle will be Jenn Schwartz, who was named executive vice president and chief strategy officer at the top of 2026. She came to ChristianaCare in 2018 to initially serve as chief legal officer. Prior to that she spent over a decade at Lourdes Health System, where she was vice president of legal affairs & general counsel as well as its executive director.

According to recent reports, > Maui Health CEO Lynn Fulton will be stepping down on May 3 after a little over two years in the Hawaiian health system's top role. She plans to return to central Illinois to be closer to her family, according to the announcement that promises a leadership transition proposal "in the coming days.".

Fulton is credited with overseeing improved quality and financial stabilization during her time at the three-hospital nonprofit system.

> Tenet Healthcare Chief Information Officer Paola Arbour plans to retire at the end of this year, according to a recent regulatory filing from the for-profit hospital and ambulatory surgical center chain. She's been in the role since 2018, and plans to stick with the organization in a part-time, non-executive role through April 1, 2028 "to provide continuing transition services and support.".

Recent findings suggest that > Samuel Marchio was named senior vice president, chief government relations and policy officer at Ascension, per a social media post. He comes off a 15-year stint at Elevance Health (initially Anthem), where most recently served as regional vice president of federal government affairs.

Industry observers note that > Stephen Taluja was named chief mission officer of Providence, a role that tasks him with aligning the Catholic nonprofit system's charity and service aims with ongoing strategic and organizational transformation. The appointment takes effect on June 29.

Taluja comes to the organization from a Bon Secours Mercy Health, where he is right now chief sponsorship and formation officer. He's been there in various roles since 2014, and before that led multicultural parish ministries.

> Addiction treatment provider Birches Health has added former Cigna Chief Medical Officer Doug Nemecek, M.D., to its advisory board as a senior adviser. As a senior adviser, Nemecek will work closely with the leadership team at Birches as it evolves its clinical and payer engagement strategies.

Nemecek's experience in the payer market will be key to informing this work, according to an announcement.

> Oraida Roman has been named as Aledade's upcoming chief commercial officer, the tech giant revealed on Wednesday. In the role, she will be tasked with leading the team's strategy around national health plan partnerships.

Roman brings 25 years of experience to the role, and will spearhead work around 200 contracts including Medicare Advantage, Medicaid and commercial plans.

> WellSpan Health President and CEO Roxanna Gapstur, Ph.D, is calling it a career after more than eight years at the nonprofit system's helm.

Industry observers note that wellSpan's board announced the aims April 6, sharing that Gapstur will continue in the role until the transition to a replacement is complete. No specific or expected timeline was given, other than sharing that a national search for that new executive has begun.

According to recent reports, the system, which employs 23,000 people, has grown under her tenure from eight hospitals to 12, and from $2.5 billion of revenue to $4.7 billion. Its footprint has also expanded from five counties to 12 across Pennsylvania and northern Maryland, now reaching more than 1 million patients.

The announcement credits Gapstur with bringing "clear strategic direction" that focused on quality, safety, patient experience and employee engagement. That approach brough national recognitions and designations to its facilities, plus newly introduced developments like a genomic program bringing precision medicine into patient care.

> Centene Corporation has created two newly introduced positions to lead key segments of its insurance business.

The tech giant mentioned in an announcement that it has named Daniel Finke as group president for markets and commercial and Michael Carson as its group president for Medicare and specialty. Both executives will report to CEO Sarah London, per Centene.

Sources indicate that finke is an experienced insurance executive and will be tasked with overseeing and scaling the tech giant's Medicaid and commercial segments. He joins the insurer from Convey Health Solutions, where he was CEO, and has also previously served as president of Aetna at CVS Health.

Carson, meanwhile, will take on an expanded role in overseeing Centene's Medicare Advantage, Part D, dual-eligible and specialty populations. He joined the tech giant as CEO of WellCare in 2024, and previously held leadership roles at Bright Healthcare and Harvard Pilgrim Health Care.

London said in the announcement that the shift recognizes Carson's significant contributions to the manufacturer and the experience that Finke brings to the table in driving operations forward.

"Their collective experience will be instrumental as we continue to strengthen performance across the portfolio and deliver sustainable, profitable growth," she said.

It has been revealed that > Cory Mead was named CEO of HCA Florida Palms West Hospital, effective March 30. With more than a decade in leadership roles with HCA Healthcare, Mead most recently served as CEO of HCA Florida Woodmont Hospital.

> Elevance Health unveiled a slew of fresh leadership appointments within its Health Benefits business and Carelon, the unit leading services such as pharmacy benefits, behavioral health and value-based care enablement.

Kristy Duffey was named president of Carelon Health. The nurse practitioner-turned-executive recently helped scale care models and boost performance at Optum and CINQCARE. She'll be taking over for Peter Haytaian, who's slated to leave the role on May 4 to focus on family commitments but will remain through the end of the year as a special advisor to ease the transition, the tech giant previously announced.

Aimée Dailey was appointed president of government business. She's already attributed with playing "a pivotal role" in expanding Elevance's government programs, and will now have responsibilities covering Medicare, Medicaid, Federal Government Solutions and Group Retiree Solutions.

Additionally, Will Feest, currently chief operating officer for Carelon, will be adding president of Carelon Insights to his title card; Darrell Oliveira was named chief financial officer for Carelon; and Jeff Plante, previously president of Carelon Insights, was dubbed chief financial officer for the Health Benefits segment.

Elevance remarked the new leaders will help expand and scale Carelon, which reaches over 90 million healthcare consumers. The Health Benefits segment provides coordinated solutions to more than 45 million Elevance members.

> Kurt Small was named president and CEO of CareFirst BlueCross BlueShield, effective May 4.

Recent findings suggest that small is at the moment president of Medicaid at Elevance Health, where he has been for nearly seven years. He has over 25 years of healthcare leadership experience, including roles at Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Minnesota, Highmark and Aetna.

Sources indicate that at Elevance, he oversaw a Medicaid business with about 8.5 million members. CareFirst, meanwhile, is a nonprofit with 3.5 million members primarily living in the District of Columbia, Maryland and Northern Virginia. It has been without a permanent top executive since last September, with Ja'Ron Bridges serving as interim president and CEO.

> Barclay Berdan, CEO of Texas Health Resources, will retire in September after four decades at the 29-hospital nonprofit.

Sources indicate that the executive stepped into his role in 2014, and was credited by the organization in its announcement release for guiding the system "through some of the most complex public health challenges in modern U.S. history while leading significant transformation across the organization’s clinical, digital and operational capabilities.".

On deck is Winjie Miao, who is currently senior executive vice president and chief operating officer. She's set for a promotion to president on April 5, priming her to step in as CEO in September when Berdan steps away. Miao has been Texas Health Resources' chief operating officer since 2022, but first joined the organization in 2000.

> Elisabeth Armstrong is the newly introduced chief of staff at the National Institutes of Health Office of the Director, filling in the void left with Seana Cranston's resignation earlier in March.

Sources indicate that armstrong, who has a doctorate in bioethics, comes from the Food and Drug Administration, where she served as director of the Office of the Executive Secretariat. Prior to joining government, she conducted healthcare policy equity research for Raymond James & Associates’ Global Equities and Investment, advised and held various ethics positions at biotech and healthcare organizations and was a broadcast journalist, among other roles.

> Cigna Healthcare, the insurance arm of the Cigna Group, announced that it named Stanley Crittenden, M.D., as its upcoming chief medical officer.

In the role, Crittenden will the lead the insurer's clinical operations, and will be tasked with partnering with other key leaders across the company to support the central goals of improving access and simplifying the healthcare journey for both patients and providers.

Crittenden brings years of experience in managed care, value-based care and population health to the role, Cigna mentioned in an announcement. He most recently served as CMO at Quantum Health, and also held leadership roles at Evergreen Nephrology, Anthem and Humana.

Crittenden is also board certified in internal medicine and nephrology, Cigna mentioned.

“I’m honored to join Cigna Healthcare at this important moment in its transformation toward making health care simpler, more personalized and more affordable,” remarked Crittenden in the announcement. “I am committed to fostering a collaborative and supportive environment, doing everything we can to improve the experience and outcomes of all those we serve.”.

> John Haupert, president and CEO of Atlanta-based Grady Health System, will be handing the reins over to current Chief Operating Officer Anthony Saul at the end of this year.

Saul is immediately claiming the president title, and will shuffle into the top spot on Jan. 1, 2027. Haupert will stick around through 2027 in an advisory role to soften the transition, support philanthropic and capital fundraising and provide strategic guidance on a new $1+ billion medical campus the nonprofit also declared this week.

Haupert has headed Grady for the past 15 years. Saul has been around for seven, initially joining as chief financial officer.

> AI-powered prior authorization company Humata Health is bringing Liz Fowler, former director of the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation (CMMI), onto its board of directors.

Recent findings suggest that the firm mentioned in an announcement that Fowler's experience at CMMI will support the team's efforts to accelerate Humata's mission to ensure patients get the care they need promptly. At CMMI, Fowler was tasked with rethinking reimbursement in Medicare and Medicaid to drive uptake of value-based care, providing critical insights she can bring to Humata.

Before her stint at CMMI, Fowler held leadership roles at the Commonwealth Fund and Johnson & Johnson. She at the moment serves as a distinguished scholar at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health and the Carey Business School.

“Liz is a unicorn, a rare leader with deep experience in all realms of the healthcare ecosystem,” said Jeremy Friese, M.D., Humata’s co-founder and CEO, in the announcement. “She understands the inherent complexities of the health system, and her expertise will be instrumental as we work toward our mission of solving these challenges.".

From her role driving innovation at CMMI to her track record of bipartisan work on federal health legislation, Liz’s experience will be an invaluable asset as we make AI-driven medical review a seamless process that ensures every patient receives the right care as quickly as possible," Friese said.

> Jeff Balser, M.D., Ph.D., is retiring from his roles as CEO of Vanderbilt Health and dean of Vanderbilt University School of Medicine at the end of 2026.

The academic system's board of directors has kicked of a national search for a successor who would hold both titles, according to the March 12 announcement.

In a recent development, A 1990 Vanderbilt graduate himself, Balser spent years as a cardiac anesthesiologist and surgical intensivist at Johns Hopkins before returning to Vanderbilt in 1998. He was named chair of the Department of Anesthesiology in 2001, dean of the medical school in 2008 and head of the Vanderbilt University Medical Center in 2009. He has served as dean and in the health system's top executive role for the past 17 years.

Recent findings suggest that the organization has grown from a four-hospital system to an eight-hospital system under his tenure, during which its annual net revenue also grew from around $2 billion to nearly $9 billion, according to the announcement. Part of that time was an effort he led to legally and financially separate the medical center and its system from the university as a standalone nonprofit. The organization's cash reserves also have also grown from 50 days to more than 110, with total cash on hand plus investments now exceeding $3 billion.

> Greg Hoffman, chief financial officer of Providence, will retire in June, the organization declared.

It has been revealed that hoffman has been with the major nonprofit system for over a decade, and served as CFO for the past five years. His tenure in the role is marked by a multi-year financial turnaround that finally brought operations into the black during the quarter ended Sept. 30, 2025. The announcement of his retirement also pointed to his role striking up new strategic partnerships, resetting contracts with commercial payers and heading the implementation of an enterprise resource planning system.

Providence said it aims to conduct an internal and national search for Hoffman's replacement.

> Kevin Tabb, M.D., president and CEO of Beth Israel Lahey Health, has given notice to the system's board that he prepares to step down after this year.

The physician executive was tapped as CEO of Beth Israel Deaconess in 2011, and stayed at the top through its merger with fellow Massachusetts provider Lahey Health in 2019. Today the organization spans 14 hospitals, employs 42,000 people and cares for 1.7 million patients annually.

Alongside navigating the merger and a pandemic, Tabb is credited with advancing initiatives around care access and connecting services delivered between its locations. Beth Israel Lahey also notched upcoming partnerships: a teaching relationship with UMass Chan School of Medicine and an upcoming cancer collaboration with the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute.

Tabb will remain in his role while the system's board searches for his successor, a process expected to take about eight to 10 months, according to the announcement.

> Health tech tech giant Stellar Health has added Raul Smith, a veteran of Elevance Health, as its chief financial officer.

Smith has 20 years of experience in healthcare leadership, according to an announcement, including six years as president CFO for Anthem's East Region. He has also served as CFO for Duo Health and Gold Kidney Health Plan.

Industry observers note that stellar noted that Smith's experience in the health insurance industry will help the organization build out its platform. Stellar supports payers in value-based care by making it easier for providers to engage with these complex environments.

In addition, he'll play a key role in driving the financial evolution of its risk-based portfolio, including the tech-enabled accountable care organization, shaco.

"Stellar is already setting the pace for value-based care, and Raul adds the institutional caliber to match our growing scale," said Michael Meng, CEO and cofounder of Stellar Health. "Raul brings the financial authority to stand behind the definitive value we deliver to our payor partners. His leadership solidifies that our ROI is absolute and verifiable—impact that will only continue to compound and get better year over year.".

> Wellpoint Tennessee, an Elevance Health subsidiary, has named Rachel Chinetti as president of its health strategy.

As president, Chinetti will be tasked with leading the insurer's strategy and operations across the state, including a focus on affordability, access and quality for individuals enrolled in TennCare, its Medicaid program.

She brings almost two decades of experience in Medicaid and long-term services and supports (LTSS) to the role, per an announcement from the insurer. Chinetti has held multiple roles within TennCare and most recently served as a staff vice president within Elevance Health's government unit, where she led a center of excellence in LTSS.

Chinetti is also a native of the state who lives in Nashville, with strong community relationships, the manufacturer remarked.

In a recent development, “It is an honor to serve Tennesseans in this role,” Chinetti said in the release. “Wellpoint Tennessee has a strong legacy of partnership and innovation. I look forward to working alongside TennCare, providers, advocates, and community leaders to strengthen rural and maternal health, enhance long-term services and supports, and deliver more coordinated, person-centered care that helps our members live healthier, more independent lives.”.

In a recent development, > James Downing, M.D., will be stepping down from his role as president and CEO of St. Jude Children's Research Hospital near the end of 2026, the pediatric research hospital unveiled.

The physician executive has been with the organization for four decades, and has sat at its head for the past 12 years. Under his leadership St. Jude underwent the largest strategic expansion in its history, which included the completion of two separate strategic plans requiring nearly $20 billion of investment and over 2,300 new positions; major expansion to St. Jude's main campus; and greater international collaboration.

Prior to that he served as scientific director for eight years, a period in which he spearheaded the Pediatric Cancer Genome Project.

Downing plans to transition into a faculty role at St. Jude's Department of Global Pediatric Medicine after handing over the reins. The organization remarked a replacement is expected to be named over the summer.

According to recent reports, “I’ve watched St. Jude transform the care of pediatric cancer around the world, and I’m grateful to have played a small part as its CEO," he said in the announcement. "It has been the honor of a lifetime to wake up every day and know that I have a purpose, to be a part of this workforce, and to change the outlook for children everywhere.”.

Recent findings suggest that >The Department of Health and Human Services revealed several leadership changes as the agency looks to advance Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s Make American Healthy Again agenda.

HHS noted that Chris Klomp will step into the role of chief counselor at the agency, where he will "oversee all operations of the department." Klomp at the moment serves as the director of Medicare.

Recent findings suggest that in addition, both Politico and the Washington Post have reported that Jim O'Neill, deputy secretary of HHS and the acting director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, will step down from both roles. Sources told the Post that O'Neill will be offered a position as an ambassador.

The Post reported that the shakeup comes amid significant controversy over the shift at HHS in vaccine policy and other hot-button topics. Kennedy is looking to shift talking points to more politically palatable topics, like healthy food, per the Post.

In addition to the new title for Klomp, Kennedy has tapped Kyle Diamantas and Grace Graham to serve as senior counselors for the Food and Drug Administration as well as John Brooks to step in as senior counselor for the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services.

HHS remarked that each of these three will also continue to hold their current roles in addition to supporting Kennedy's office.

"I am proud to elevate battle-tested, principled leaders onto my immediate team—individuals with the courage and experience to help us move faster and go further as we work to Make America Healthy Again," Kennedy stated in the press release.

>The Federation of American Hospitals announced multiple leadership appointments this week.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
CMS proposes sweeping Medicare integrity rule it says will save $90B" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services rolled out a newly introduced proposed rule it said could save $90 billion over ten years through increased oversight and prevention of fraud and improper payments.

It has been revealed that the Comprehensive Regulations to Uncover Suspicious Healthcare (CRUSH) proposed rule, shared late Monday, spans Medicare, Medicaid, the Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) and the Health Insurance Marketplace. It follows a request for information the administration circulated back in February. CMS it intends to conduct similar program integrity rulemaking “on an annual basis going forward.”.

Among the highlights: stiffer provider screening and safeguards for Medicare enrollment, a latest regulatory framework for reporting and returning self-identified Medicaid fee-for-service overpayments similar to those in other programs, and requirements that Medicaid managed care plans report beneficiary deaths or address changes within 30 days to help CMS better spot improper payments.

“When President Trump called upon the federal government to crush fraud, waste, and abuse, CMS got right to work, using every tool at its disposal to achieve historic savings,” CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, M.D., said in the agency’s announcement of the proposed rule. “CRUSH would build on those results by giving us stronger tools to prevent fraud, remove bad actors, and protect the Americans who rely on these programs. Whether criminals are billing Medicare for nonexistent canes and wheelchairs, fraudulently enrolling healthy seniors in Medicare-funded hospice care, or signing people up for Marketplace plans without their consent, the CRUSH proposed rule would give CMS stronger authority to stop these schemes and hold those responsible accountable.”.

The additional guardrails are expected to cost the government about $378.5 million over the same 10-year period CMS expects to save nearly $90 billion, according to the proposed rule.

Industry observers note that CMS, in its release and a lengthy fact sheet outlining the proposed changes, said it wants to upgrade Medicare provisions to tighten Medicare Advantage (MA) Adjustment Data Validation audits so that it can better spot cases in which diagnoses are not supported by medical documentation, thereby bumping up risk scores and payments. It also wants to increase suspicious activity reporting requirements for MA organizations and Part D plan sponsors, require some MA plan providers and suppliers to also enroll in Original Medicare for credential verification and guard seniors from unsolicited outreach from medical supply companies.

Recent findings suggest that in Medicaid and CHIP, the agency wants to make it easier for states to join in on suspected schemes while fleshing out their data collection and reporting. CMS also wants to add provider enrollment termination grounds similar to those in Medicare.

According to recent reports, within the marketplace, CMS said it wants to begin restricting access for agents and brokers with certain felony convictions or other healthcare program exclusions on their record. The agency is also looking to bolster its authority to suspend and terminate, and to do so more swiftly.

Recent findings suggest that “President Trump directed us to stop fraud, waste, and abuse, and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services is taking action to protect taxpayer dollars,” HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. remarked in the announcement. “CRUSH would give CMS stronger tools to block fraudulent payments, remove dishonest providers, and protect Americans from schemes that exploit their healthcare coverage.

Industry observers note that public comment on the proposed rule, which includes more potential changes and a breakdown of the expected savings and costs, will be open through Jan. 19, 2027.

The program integrity proposed rule landed the same day CMS released its estimates on improper payments during fiscal year 2026.

In a recent development, improper payments are those that do not meet the agency’s program requirements, and can include overpayments or underpayments alike. They are not necessarily a measure of fraud, though “some improper payments may involve fraud or abuse” alongside administrative errors, CMS said.

In total, the agency outlined about $112.9 billion in estimated overpayments, an increase over the roughly $96.1 billion estimated for the prior fiscal year. That broke down into:.

CMS noted that the estimates are tied to claims submitted from July 1, 2024 through June 30, 2025, a period “before many of CMS’ current crushing fraud initiatives were implemented.” Those and other efforts will begin appearing in next year’s improper payment data, it mentioned.

Sources indicate that google's newly introduced Ask Maps feature uses its Gemini AI to lay out an entire itinerary for your next trip in Google Maps, whether it's a day-long adventure, to a journey of several days. Obviously the announcement was timed to provide enough runway for people to put it to use for the upcoming holiday season in the U.S. AAA expects 81.5 million people to travel for the Thanksgiving and the capitalism-fueled Black Friday holiday weekend.

Recent findings suggest that to get started, all you have to do is Ask Maps to plan your trip for so many days and suggest what you'd like to do for the trip. Google puts it like this:.

In a recent development, use Ask Maps to strategy a day trip for holiday shopping or something more complex — like a three-day road trip with stops for coastal hikes and oceanfront dining. You'll get a day-by-day schedule with insider tips and numbered map pins for each stop, making it easy to visualize the plan. Once you're happy with the itinerary, share it with friends and family, or export it to Google Docs on desktop.

According to recent reports, it's that easy. This could be handy for planning a long trip with an electric vehicle and get help with finding charging stations. Or planning that automotive day trip in Detroit. From my quick search, it could use some edits.

In a recent development, in the U.S. you can modify your itinerary in real-time. If some place ends up closed, or you need to make a detour or additional stop, Ask Maps to add or adjust accordingly. It'll also make appointments for you. Need an upcoming day off to be filled with appointments and errands or just let it order the takeout you wanted instead of using whatever other delivery apps are on your phone. Ask Maps will do it all. The only finger you may have to lift is the one typing in the query to Ask Maps to do the work for you. Although, to be honest, you're more likely to ask it to do the task via voice command.

According to recent reports, perhaps the most curious thought surrounding this, aside from humanity's continued loss of curiosity and self-sufficiency while letting Google do the work, is how long will Google serve these trip recommendations organically? It really is only a matter of time before Google feeds destinations and appointments paid for by the highest bidder like it has with its Search results, or in Google Maps (no Google, I do not want to eat Chick-fil-A, nor do I want to eat it at 8 a.m. in a snowstorm on my way to a doctor's appointment).

Sources indicate that lucky for the world, this feature is expected to expand to Google Maps in over 30 countries across Europe and approximately 200 countries and territories, so everyone can melt their brains by letting Google tell it how to do even more things. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Regulators approve fresh agreement to ensure data centers pay for their own energy costs.
  • In a recent development, SALEM, Oregon — The Oregon Public Utility Commission has approved an agreement between advocates and Pacific Power.
  • 1, 2027, new Pacific Power data centers will be held responsible for their own energy costs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Regulators approve fresh agreement to ensure data centers pay for their own energy costs.

In a recent development, SALEM, Oregon — The Oregon Public Utility Commission has approved an agreement between advocates and Pacific Power. Now, Pacific Power customers have a strong suite of protections against data centers’ impact on Oregonians’ energy bills.

Starting Jan. 1, 2027, new Pacific Power data centers will be held responsible for their own energy costs. These new rules will only apply to future data centers and existing ones making significant investments, which regulators identified as the most pressing challenge to address. Right now, the utility has very few existing data centers on its system.

“With a long line of data centers waiting at Pacific Power’s door, I’m confident that we have the right protections at the right time,” remarked Bob Jenks, Executive Director of Oregon Citizens’ Utility Board. “We were able to stop more extreme impacts on power bills just in time.”.

In a recent development, data centers over 100 MW will also have to pay a small surcharge to fund energy efficiency upgrades for low-income households. This includes funding for deep home retrofits, lowering energy use across the grid while saving customers on monthly bills.

“Many of the households we serve are already struggling to afford their energy bills and risk having their utilities shut off. Data centers will help fund weatherization, energy efficiency upgrades, and the critical home repairs that often prevent our clients from accessing these improvements in the first place,” remarked Charity Fain, Executive Director of Community Energy Project. “Requiring data centers to cover the costs of the energy infrastructure they need, rather than passing those costs on to residential customers, is an important protection for low-income households, seniors, and people with disabilities.”.

It has been revealed that under this order, if there is a power emergency, Pacific Power can prioritize critical energy use for other customers, like renters and homeowners, by curtailing service to data centers. Increased electric demand by data centers strains the grid and increases the potential for blackouts during heat waves or hard freezes.

Recent findings suggest that “This is a big win that puts Oregon at the forefront of managing data center growth the right way,” remarked Joshua Basofin, Oregon Clean Energy Program Director at Climate Solutions. “It protects Oregonians from rising costs and strengthens grid resilience. Data centers should not harm our ability to access essential electricity to power our lives and keep us safe all year.”.

Regulators also ruled that latest data centers can only be connected to Pacific Power’s grid if there is enough emissions-free electricity available to serve them. Under HB 2021, Pacific Power is required by law to serve all customers with 100% emissions-free electricity by 2040. This new rule will help manage costs for other customers outside of data centers during the transition to clean energy.

“We have long known that clean energy is the most affordable form of energy,” stated Ben Brint, Senior Climate Program Director at Oregon Environmental Council. “This ruling is a win for data center accountability, and for Oregonians across the state — especially frontline communities already bearing the brunt of climate impacts and rising energy costs. It will save ratepayers money in the short and long run, allocating costs appropriately while advancing Oregon’s 100% clean energy goals.”.

Recent findings suggest that this change also comes at a time when many Oregonians are calling for broader changes to how the state handles data centers. Impacts on data centers are poised to be an matter again at the Oregon State Legislature in 2027.

“The POWER Act demonstrated the people’s power to fight back against the rising energy rates and ecosystem harms that large data centers inflict,” remarked Emily Bowes, Policy Strategist & Acting Director at Sierra Club Oregon. “In 2027, alongside latest and returning climate champions, we will continue to fight for a clean energy transition in Salem and statewide.”.

In a recent development, in 2025, the Oregon Legislature passed the POWER Act to help utilities rein in data centers’ added costs to Oregonians’ energy bills. Last fall, Portland General Electric began the work to roll out this new law in practice. In January, Pacific Power started a similar process for its customers. The next step is to address the few existing data centers on Pacific Power’s system, starting as early as summer 2027. It is unclear if the final phase will include rate adjustments.
